newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma says new phase begins as PM quits.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma says new phase begins as PM quits.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma accepted the resignation of his controversial prime minister on Wednesday and declared economic reforms would move faster.

"Kuchma said a new phase in the activity of the government had begun and that reforms would now be carried out more actively," spokesman Dmytro Markov quoted Kuchma as telling a senior German Christian Democrat visiting Kiev.
"Government itself should be restructured as well," Markov said, quoting Kuchma, who earlier accepted Pavlo Lazarenko's resignation.
The president has said the number of government officials should be reduced by a third to make their work more efficient.

The International Monetary Fund warned after parliament passed the budget six months into the year that the former Soviet republic may have to wait for a $2.5-$3 billion, three-year loan for countries undertaking structural reforms.
The Fund said a second, interim stand-by deal may be issued instead until Ukraine meets about 10 outstanding conditions.
Kuchma had come under increasing pressure from Western and Ukrainian officials to remove Lazarenko, accused of being partly to blame for sluggish reforms especially in privatisation.
Western media have said Lazarenko was behind Ukraine's biggest gas trader, the United Energy Systems of Ukraine, and alleged that he received $200 million in revenues.
He was the initiator and backer of a scheme introduced in 1995 which involved private companies distributing gas on the Ukrainian market. He denies any personal gain.
The decision, which followed months of speculation about Lazarenko's links to the energy sector, means Kuchma will have to re-appoint the entire cabinet within 60 days.
A spokesman for Kuchma said Lazarenko's deputy Vasyl Durdynets had been re-appointed acting prime minister and Kuchma had decreed the cabinet should keep working in the meantime.
Kuchma issued a decree on June 19 appointing Durdynets acting prime minister because of Lazarenko's health, a move which was seen as heralding his departure from power.

Some aides said Lazarenko's health was fine, one said he was suffering from "exhaustion" and the chief doctor at the hospital where he has been a patient ever since said he was suffering from a severe form of varicose veins.
Kuchma will need approval from 226 deputies in the 450-seat parliament for any candidate, and several names have come up.

They include Anatoly Kinakh, head of the Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, and Serhiy Tyhypko, deputy minister in charge of reforms, who has an image as a youthful reformer able to boost Ukraine's standing abroad.

But Tyhypko, 37, a former banker who was attending an investment conference in Frankfurt, made clear in an interview with Reuters he thought he was too young, joking: "I think it's better not to have a country full of green prime ministers".
Kuchma's chief-of-staff has been lobbying for Oleh Dyomin, a regional governor, sources close to his administration say.
Local media have said Olexander Tkachenko, a prominent leftist in parliament, could also be in the running.
Several deputies said earlier that they wanted someone "simple", lacking the political ambitions of his predecessor and able to push through reforms to take Lazarenko's place.
They said it was important to name someone quickly as parliament's political loyalties can change from day to day.
One favourite was Ivan Plyushch, a former parliamentary speaker under Kuchma's predecessor with a reputation for wit, uttering "folksy" Ukrainian sayings and being a centrist.
One analyst recalled him asking a small, nationalist deputy in parliament whose surname in Ukrainian "Zayets" means "hare" to "stop hopping around the chamber".
